title: You Can See Everything
dek: Nathan Fielder moved in with Elizabeth Holmes for her last 34 days of freedom. Three years and 174 minutes later, nobody can agree on what happened in that house. It's the most talked-about documentary of the year, and it's playing on Queen Anne right now.
body: Here's a pitch no sane studio would greenlight. Take the most famous fraudster of the decade in the weeks before she reports to federal prison. Let her and her partner invite a film crew into their rented beach house north of San Diego so the world can finally see the real her. Then hand the camera to Nathan Fielder, the deadpan maniac behind Nathan for You, The Rehearsal and The Curse. A24 made it. It opened Friday. And it is, depending on who you ask, either a masterpiece or the smuggest thing in theaters.
## How it happened

The origin story depends on who's telling it. One version says Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim reached out after a friend mentioned Holmes was looking for someone to document her life. At an Academy Museum Q&A, the filmmakers said it was the other way around: Holmes went to A24 first, after watching a Nathan for You clip on YouTube. Her partner, Billy Evans, had seen Oppenheim's retirement-community doc Some Kind of Heaven and didn't think much of its opening. A24 gave them a budget and an exit if nothing came of it.

Something came of it. The crew lived with Holmes, Evans and their two small kids for the 34 days before she reported to prison on May 30, 2023. Fielder held out on moving in until the last two weeks. The whole project ran about three years and stayed secret until a month before its premiere.

That premiere was a surprise screening at Telluride on September 6. Phones were locked in pouches. Security stood by in night-vision goggles. Fielder told the crowd afterward that he's still struggling to understand what he experienced.
## The promise

The title is the couple's own pitch: radical transparency. You can see everything. Holmes, who is serving time for defrauding investors in her blood-testing company Theranos, tells the camera she has never told a lie, not even a white one. When Fielder pushes, she asks the question the whole movie hangs on.
> Why would I deceive you? (Elizabeth Holmes, in the film)

Fielder doesn't play journalist or science expert. He hovers in the background with headphones and a monitor, asks simple questions, and keeps asking until something makes sense or someone interrupts. Then he lets the silence sit there until it gets unbearable.
## The scenes people can't stop talking about

He plays the couple Abbott and Costello's 'Who's on First?' on YouTube. WBUR's Sean Burns says Holmes stares at it with no apparent comprehension. Evans takes a bowl of raw eggs out of her hands to show her the correct way to mix them. The family digs the old Theranos device out of the garage and works the phones with investors for a new blood-testing venture that uses lasers; Evans's real company has publicly insisted it is not Theranos 2.0. Holmes can't finish watching The Dropout and objects to how it shows her device failing.

Then there's the 2023 New York Times profile. The couple fixate on one line in it, about the public seeing a character she created. They swear she was misquoted and say they have a recording that proves it. They won't let Fielder hear it. The Times stands by its story.

About halfway through, Holmes reports to prison, and the movie turns into something else. The family moves to Texas. Fielder buys jerky from a prison vending machine. Amanda Seyfried, who won an Emmy playing Holmes, and Christopher Abbott show up to reenact scenes in the same house, and Seyfried coaches Fielder for his prison visits. Slate calls her performance astonishing. There's a confrontation in a WeWork in South Austin. There is also a late twist that A24 begged critics not to spoil. We won't either.
## The critics are losing their minds
It's at 99 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from more than 100 reviews, with audiences at 99 too. Metacritic has it at 99, with no mixed or negative reviews counted. IMDb users rate it 9.3.

The AP's Lindsey Bahr gave it four stars out of four and called it a staggering piece of performance art. The Guardian gave it five and called it a gloriously destabilizing hall of psychological mirrors. Rolling Stone called it simply, unabashedly brilliant. The Seattle Times' Moira Macdonald put it plainly: it's a great one. The Globe and Mail called it the greatest movie of the year. The Free Beacon's review was two words: holy cow.
## Not everybody's buying it

TIME's Stephanie Zacharek panned it. She found the first half smug, the style pure snark, and the whole thing more like a product brought to market than a reinvention of anything Frederick Wiseman or the Maysles brothers did. The Austin Chronicle flagged what it called a serious breach of documentary ethics that the film treats as a subplot. Next Best Picture says it has blind spots, especially around the real victims, the patients and investors Theranos burned.

Then there are the fair questions. The couple clearly hoped the film would rehabilitate Holmes and help their startup. Her two small kids are underfoot through much of it. The Ringer points out she didn't even know the filmmakers' work until someone showed her YouTube clips. And Awards Daily's Sasha Stone, who loved the movie, argues the edit turns Evans into the villain and makes the audience complicit in what the film does to Holmes. Critics do pile on Evans: the Boston Globe calls him a classic manipulator, SlashFilm calls him possibly the most heinous villain of 2026.
## What the filmmakers say
> If we can't agree on what's happening, there's something here. (Nathan Fielder, NYFF Q&A)

Fielder says communication with the couple broke down near the end, and that Evans tried to control the process. Oppenheim says neither Holmes nor Evans has seen the finished film. Evans, on the All-In podcast, admitted he hadn't watched it and might think it's the dumbest thing he's ever done.
## Where she is now

Holmes is at a federal prison camp in Bryan, Texas. Her original sentence was 11 years and 3 months. A judge cut a year in March after a sentencing-rule change, and her projected release is now February 2030, with a halfway house in the Austin area approved for August 2027. She has a commutation request pending with the Trump administration. She and her former partner Sunny Balwani still owe $452 million in restitution. Theranos once raised about $945 million at a $9 billion valuation before the Wall Street Journal blew it open in 2015.
## The money

For a documentary, the box office is bananas. Thursday previews brought in about $1.7 million, a number TheWrap called unheard of for a doc. Deadline is projecting around $12 million for the weekend, which would be the biggest opening for a non-music documentary in a decade. It goes nationwide on October 23.
## Where to see it in Seattle

SIFF Cinema Uptown on Queen Anne opened it Friday, and Saturday night's 7 p.m. show sold out. Regal Meridian downtown is running it all day. Majestic Bay in Ballard picks it up October 22, and the Tasveer Film Center in Columbia City runs it October 23 to 27.
## The Sinner's take

Go. Go cold, skip the trailers, and don't let anybody spoil it. A grifter, a prankster and a camera locked in a beach house is the best horror movie of the month, and it isn't even a horror movie. Bring a friend so you have somebody to argue with on the walk home. Then come back here and argue with everyone else.
